Labor
LAY-bur
v.
Latin laborare, “to work, toil.” Renders the Greek kopiaō, “to grow weary by toil, labor to weariness,” and ergāzomai, “to work”; and the Hebrew ‘āmal, “to labor, toil,” and yāga, “to be weary, work hard.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To labor, in Scripture’s ministerial and spiritual register, is the wearying, sustained, costly work of the saint and the minister in the things of God: the labor of preaching, of prayer, of pastoral care, of the daily mortification of sin, of bearing burdens in the body of Christ, and of the manual labor by which the believer eats his own bread and gives to him that needeth. The Greek kopiaō is the most freighted of the verbs: it does not simply mean to work; it means to work to weariness, to labor until tired. Paul saturates his ministry-language with it: therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God; I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me; let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine; greet Mary, who bestowed much labour on us; my beloved brother and labourer with me in the gospel; and the great closing verse of 1 Corinthians 15: therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. Christ Himself uses the verb pastorally in His invitation: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; and in His sending: the harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few; pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send forth labourers into his harvest. The biblical labour is therefore weighty work, deliberately undertaken, sustained over time, often to the point of exhaustion, and grounded in the assurance that in the Lord it is not in vain. The contrast in Scripture is sharp: labor in the Lord versus labor in the flesh (the latter being the wearying striving that achieves nothing because not grounded in grace); labor in the Lord versus idleness (the avoidance of labor that Paul roundly condemns in 2 Thess 3); and labor in the Lord versus the world’s labor for what perisheth (against which Christ commands, labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LABOR as exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; particularly, the exertion of the limbs in occupations by which subsistence is obtained, as in agriculture and manufactures; toil; work; pains.

expand to see more

LABOR, v.i. — 1. To exert muscular strength; to act or move with painful effort, particularly in service to another, or in any employment for hire. 2. To exert mental powers, in the performance of any business; to study; to take pains. 3. To toil; to be burdened. 4. To be in distress; to be pressed; to suffer.

LABOR, v.t. — To work at; to till; to cultivate. The husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits (2 Tim 2:6).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 15:58 — "Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord."

Matthew 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

1 Timothy 5:17 — "Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine."

John 6:27 — "Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give unto you..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Christian labor is corrupted, on one side, by the comfort-and-balance register of contemporary middle-class faith that recoils from any labor sustained to weariness, treating exhaustion in the Lord’s work as poor self-care—and on the other by the flesh-driven workaholism that labors much but not in the Lord, and so is exhausted but not fruitful.

expand to see more

The contemporary register of comfort and balance recoils from the New Testament’s constant language of labor to weariness. Paul saying he laboured more abundantly than they all; Epaphras always labouring fervently for you in prayers; the elders to be honored especially for laboring in the word and doctrine; Mary who bestowed much labour on us; the apostle’s closing charge to abound in the work of the Lord because your labour is not in vain in the Lord—all of this sits uncomfortably with a Christianity that has absorbed the broader culture’s suspicion of any exhaustion in service. Exhaustion is reflexively treated as a failure of self-care; sustained labor in the Lord’s work is recast as unhealthy boundaries; the apostolic register is, in practice, set aside. Scripture is sharper. The Christian life is, in a real sense, a life of labor—labor to weariness, labor that costs, labor sustained over years. The grace that grounds it makes the labor possible and joyful, but does not eliminate the labor itself.

The opposite corruption is the flesh-driven workaholism that labors much without laboring in the Lord. Activity replaces dependence; energy replaces grace; the minister or saint runs hard but in his own strength, and the result is exhaustion without proportionate fruit, and often a slow embittering as the labor goes unacknowledged and the strength fails. Paul’s own qualification is essential: I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. The two clauses must stand together. Recover both ends. Refuse the comfort-and-balance retreat from sustained labor in the Lord, and refuse the flesh-driven labor that is not grounded in grace. The biblical pattern is sustained, costly, weariness-touching labor done in the Lord by the grace of God—and Scripture’s assurance to those who labor in that pattern is firm: your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kopiaō (to grow weary by toil) and ergāzomai (to work); Hebrew ‘āmal (to labor) and yāga (to be weary, work hard)—the wearying, sustained, costly work of saint and minister, grounded in grace and never in vain in the Lord.

expand to see more

Greek kopiaō (G2872) — to grow weary, labor to the point of fatigue (the freighted ministry-verb).

Greek kopos (G2873) — labor, trouble, toil (the noun).

Greek ergāzomai (G2038) — to work (the broader verb).

Hebrew ‘āmal (H6001) — to labor, toil; the noun ‘āmāl means “labor, trouble.”

Usage

"Your labour is not in vain in the Lord—the great closing assurance of 1 Cor 15 grounds every sustained Christian exertion."

"Paul’s qualification stands: I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me."

"Comfort-and-balance recoils from labor to weariness; flesh-driven workaholism labors without grace—biblical labor is sustained, costly, and in the Lord."
